teaser: For 250 years her paintings hung under other men's names. Here she tells you who made them.
review_notes:
Opening: Google Doodle honoring Judith Leyster, 19 December 2022. Please verify the date and that the drawing showed her at an easel.
Date of the painting about 1630; 74.6 x 65.1 cm; National Gallery of Art, Washington, acquired 1949 (gift of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Woods Bliss). The canvas was long attributed to Frans Hals before being recognized as hers.
Infrared examination (NGA): the canvas on the easel first showed a young woman's face, later replaced by the fiddler, who also appears in her Merry Company of about 1630.
Number of brushes in her left hand: commonly given as eighteen; the lesson says 'about eighteen'.
Admitted to the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke in 1633, among the first women registered there as master painters.
1635 dispute: a pupil left her for Hals's workshop; she complained to the guild, which awarded her part of the fee and fined Hals. Simplified.
Family name taken from the father's brewery, 'Leyster' (lodestar); monogram JL with a star.
Married the painter Jan Miense Molenaer in 1636; few later works known; died 1660.
1893: a painting bought by the Louvre as a Hals (The Carousing Couple, also called The Happy Couple) was found to carry her monogram under a false Hals signature; Cornelis Hofstede de Groot then published the first group of her works. A lawsuit between dealers preceded this in London.
The idea that the picture was a showpiece for clients or for the guild is a hypothesis; stated as 'may'.

lesson.text: On December 19, 2022, people around the world opened Google and found a little drawing above the search bar: a woman from the 1600s at her easel. Many clicked on it to learn who she was. Her name was Judith Leyster, and for most of the time since her death almost nobody could have told them.

This is how she introduced herself, around 1630, at about twenty-one. She leans back, one elbow hooked over her chair, and turns from her work as if you had just come into the studio. Her lips are parted. She does not look interrupted. She looks pleased that you came.

lesson.title: A first impression
lesson.text: Everything in the pose is chosen to tell you something about her. Three places to check.

spots.title: About to speak
spots.text: The mouth is open, the teeth just visible. Portraits of the time usually keep lips shut. She paints herself as good company, quick and talkative.

spots.title: The collar
spots.text: A stiff disc of linen edged with lace, wide as her shoulders. Nobody paints in this. One drop of oil would ruin it. It is there to show she can afford it, and can paint it.

spots.title: The elbow
spots.text: Her arm rests on the chair back, pushing toward us out of the picture. A casual pose like this was something male painters used in their own portraits, to look at ease and in command.

lesson.text: So the working clothes are a fiction and the ease is real. The picture is an advertisement, and a clever one. It may have been made to show clients, or the painters' guild, the trade association that decided who was allowed to sell pictures in town. It displays her face, her manners and her skill in one object.

Her family name came from a beer. Her father ran a Haarlem brewery called the Leyster, meaning lodestar, the star sailors steer by. She turned it into a signature: her initials, J and L, joined to a small shooting star.

She was born in Haarlem in 1609, the eighth child of that brewer, who later went bankrupt. A girl from such a family did not normally become a painter: most women artists of the time were daughters of painters and learned at home. In 1633 Leyster entered the Haarlem guild as a master, among the very first women to do so, and took on pupils of her own.
Now look at what she chose to put on the easel. A portraitist advertising herself might show a portrait. She shows a laughing musician instead, and she aims her brush at him like a pointer.
Two thin sticks cross the right half of the picture, and one slope answers them.

lines.label: Her brush
lines.text: The brush runs from her fingers straight down to the fiddler's legs, where its tip nearly touches the canvas. It ties the maker to the thing made.

lines.label: His bow
lines.text: The fiddler holds his bow just as she holds her brush, between thumb and fingers. Two performers, each with a tool, each smiling at an audience.

lines.label: The lean
lines.text: From the elbow on the chair up to her head, her body slopes back, away from the easel and toward you. She points at the canvas but gives her attention to the visitor: the customer comes first.

lesson.text: The fiddler was a second sales pitch. Leyster's best sellers were not portraits but lively scenes of musicians, drinkers and children, and this very figure appears in one of them, a merry company she painted around the same time. In a single frame she says: I do faces, and I do these.

The fiddler was a change of plan. Infrared images, which let researchers see beneath the top layer of paint, show that the canvas on the easel first held a young woman's face. Leyster painted over it. A portrait inside a portrait was less useful to her than a sample of her popular work.
A self-portrait is rarely just a likeness. This one is a business card: it shows who she is, how she behaves and what she sells.
The left hand finishes the argument. Low in the corner, where it is easy to miss, she has piled up the equipment of the trade.
Her right hand holds one brush. Where does she keep the others?

spots.title: A fistful of brushes
spots.text: Her left hand grips a palette dotted with fresh paint, a white rag, and a whole bundle of brushes, about eighteen. One brush per color means no time lost cleaning. This is a professional's setup.

lesson.text: She was not shy about her rights either. In 1635 one of her pupils left her to work in the studio of Frans Hals, the most famous painter in town. Leyster complained to the guild. It awarded her part of the fee she was owed and fined Hals.

The next year she married another painter, Jan Miense Molenaer. They moved to Amsterdam and had five children, and she seems to have painted very little afterward. She died in 1660. Within a generation her name had dropped out of the books, and her pictures were sold as the work of her husband or of Hals. This self-portrait, too, was long believed to be by Hals.

A forged signature brought her back. In 1893 the Louvre in Paris bought a painting of a happy couple as a Frans Hals. Under the false Hals signature someone noticed a monogram: a J, an L and a star. A Dutch scholar followed the clue and reassembled the first small group of her paintings.

Which brings back that search page in 2022. Leyster built this picture so that a stranger would remember her name. It took about three and a half centuries longer than she planned, and several million clicks, but the advertisement finally worked.

quiz.question: Why is the huge lace collar surprising?
options: It was worn only by men
Nobody would wear it to paint: it shows status, not real working dress
It was added by a later owner
quiz.explanation: The fine clothes are for show, since oil paint would ruin them.

quiz.question: What did infrared images find under the fiddler on the easel?
quiz.explanation: Leyster first painted a woman's face there, then replaced it with the musician.

quiz.question: Where did the name Leyster come from?
options: Her father's brewery, named after the lodestar
quiz.explanation: The brewery was called the Leyster, and she signed with a star.

quiz.question: What happened when a pupil left her for Hals's studio?
options: She complained to the guild, which fined Hals
She went to work for Hals too
quiz.explanation: The guild awarded her part of the fee and fined Hals.

quiz.question: How was she rediscovered in 1893?
options: Her monogram was found under a false Hals signature
Her diary was found in an attic
quiz.explanation: A painting bought by the Louvre as a Hals turned out to carry her J, L and star.

facts.text: Leyster was the daughter of a well-known painter.
facts.explanation: Her father was a brewer, which made her career unusual.

facts.text: The fiddler on the easel also appears in another painting by Leyster.
facts.explanation: He comes from one of her merry companies, the kind of scene she sold best.

facts.text: She kept painting a great deal after her marriage.
facts.explanation: After marrying Molenaer in 1636 she seems to have painted very little.
